hook.text: Sticky, mushy or burnt rice at the bottom of the pot: almost everyone has been there. The fix is simpler than you think. In seven steps, you'll cook fluffy rice with separate grains, using only a pot, a lid and a stove, every single time. And if a batch goes wrong, I'll show you how to rescue it.

intro.text: Rice goes wrong for a few simple reasons. Too much water, too much stirring, too much heat, or a lid lifted at the wrong time. Once you know the rules, rice is one of the easiest foods you can cook, and it costs almost nothing. We'll use plain long-grain white rice as our example, and I'll tell you how to adapt for basmati, jasmine and brown rice along the way. It is a method you will use for the rest of your life.

youneed.text: Here's what you need. Long-grain white rice. A medium pot with a tight-fitting lid, since the lid is the key to steam. A measuring cup. A fine mesh strainer, or just a bowl. A fork for fluffing at the end. And a pinch of salt, if you like. A kitchen scale is optional, because a simple cup is enough.

step-1.text: Step one. Use a measuring cup to measure your rice, and remember the number, because the water will be based on it. One cup of dry rice makes about three cups cooked, which feeds two to three people. Choose a pot that suits the amount, since a pot that is too big dries the rice out, and a pot that is too small boils over. A heavy-bottomed pot spreads the heat more evenly and helps prevent burning. Take a moment to read the instructions on your package, because different varieties of rice have slightly different needs. Measuring takes ten seconds and removes the guesswork.

step-2.text: Step two. Put the rice in a strainer or a bowl, and rinse it under cold running water, swishing it with your fingers. The water will start out milky. That cloudiness is surface starch, and it is what makes rice clump and turn gummy. Keep rinsing for about a minute, until the water runs mostly clear. Drain well, and shake off the excess water. Rinsing matters most for basmati and jasmine, while rice that is labelled pre-washed or enriched should not be rinsed. Check the packet if you are unsure. Good rinsing is the difference between restaurant rice and cafeteria rice.

step-3.text: Step three. For long-grain white rice, the classic ratio is one cup of rice to one and a half cups of water. Basmati and jasmine are similar, around one to one and a quarter or one and a half. Brown rice needs more, about one to two, and a longer cooking time. Add a pinch of salt, and, if you wish, a small knob of butter or a teaspoon of oil. Always check the instructions on the packet first, since brands differ. The ratio is the secret, so measure it, and don't eyeball it. If you prefer softer rice, add a tablespoon more water, but never much more.

step-4.text: Step four. Put the pot on high heat, with the lid off, and bring it to a full boil. As soon as the water bubbles, give the rice a single stir to loosen anything stuck to the bottom, and then don't stir it again. Stirring rice releases starch, which makes it creamy and sticky, great for risotto, but not for fluffy rice. Be ready to move to the next step right away, because the water must not boil away without the lid. It takes only a few minutes to get this far. Use a timer on your phone, and don't walk too far from the kitchen.

step-5.text: Step five. Turn the heat down to the lowest setting, cover the pot with the tight lid, and set a timer for fifteen minutes. White long-grain rice usually needs fifteen to eighteen minutes, brown rice around forty-five. Do not lift the lid during this time. The rice cooks in the trapped steam, and every peek lets heat and moisture escape, which leaves you with hard, uneven grains. If your lid is loose, place a clean tea towel under it. If your stove runs hot, use a heat diffuser. A tight lid is non-negotiable, so choose a pot that closes well.

step-6.text: Step six. When the timer rings, turn off the heat, but keep the lid on, and let the pot sit for ten minutes. This resting time is as important as cooking. The steam spreads evenly through the pot, and the moisture at the bottom is absorbed, so the grains firm up and stop being sticky. Move the pot to a cool burner if you have an electric stove, because the hot ring will keep cooking the bottom. Don't skip it, even when you are hungry and dinner is waiting. Many people think this step is optional, but it is where the texture is decided.

step-7.text: Step seven. Remove the lid and gently fluff the rice with a fork, lifting it from the bottom and folding it over. A spoon crushes the grains, but a fork keeps them separate and light. Serve it while it is hot. Leftover rice needs care, because it can carry bacteria that survive cooking. Cool it within one hour, spread out on a tray if you can, then refrigerate it in a covered container and eat it within a day. When reheating, make sure it is steaming hot all the way through. A small splash of water helps in the microwave.

step-8.text: Rice went wrong? Most of it can be saved. If it is mushy, spread it on a tray to dry, or turn it into fried rice. If it is hard in the middle, add two or three tablespoons of water, cover the pot, and steam it on very low heat for a few minutes. If the bottom is burnt, do not scrape it. Spoon out the good rice from the top.

step-9.text: Plain rice is only the start. Toast the dry rice in a little oil for a minute before adding the water, which gives a nutty taste. Cook it in stock instead of water, or drop in a bay leaf or a cinnamon stick. After fluffing, fold in lemon zest or fresh herbs. For fried rice, use rice cooked and chilled the day before.

step-10.text: A burnt pot is easy to avoid. Use a heavy-bottomed pot with a tight lid, and keep the heat as low as it will go. Set a timer, so you never have to guess. If you cook a larger amount, use a bigger pot and add a few extra minutes. If rice does stick, soak the pot in hot soapy water for half an hour.

mistakes.text: Now, the three mistakes that turn rice into mush. First, skipping the rinse, which leaves too much starch. Second, adding too much water, or measuring by eye. A little extra water is the most common reason for soggy rice. And third, lifting the lid or stirring while it cooks. Every peek lets out the steam, and every stir makes it sticky. Remember also that leftover rice should never sit out on the counter for hours. Cool it quickly and refrigerate it.

recap.text: Let's recap. Measure your rice and pick the right pot. Rinse until the water runs clear. Use the right water ratio. Bring it to a boil and stir just once. Cover and simmer on low without peeking. Rest it off the heat for ten minutes. And fluff it with a fork, then store leftovers safely. Seven steps, about thirty minutes, and fluffy rice every time. The bonus sections cover rescuing rice, flavor and burnt pots.

outro.text: That's how you cook rice perfectly on the stove. If your rice turned out fluffy, subscribe to WikiTube, because we publish a new how-to every single day. Tell us in the comments what you serve with your rice, and what you would like us to explain next. See you tomorrow.

short-hook.text: Fluffy rice every time, with three simple rules.

short-step-1.text: One. Rinse the rice until the water runs mostly clear.

short-step-2.text: Two. Use one cup of rice to one and a half cups of water. Boil, stir once, cover, and simmer on low.

short-step-3.text: Three. Don't lift the lid. Rest off the heat for ten minutes, then fluff with a fork.

short2-hook.text: Stop lifting the lid on your rice.

short2-beat-1.text: Every peek lets the steam out, so the rice cooks unevenly and turns mushy.

short2-beat-2.text: Cover it, turn the heat to low, and don't touch it. Then rest it ten minutes off the heat.
